general.description: Rock-like xenobiological organisms that resemble eroded mineral formations. They grow as semi-solid exoskeletal structures emerging from rocky terrain, often mistaken for geological features. They thrive in low-atmosphere environments and exhibit slow mineral accretion growth.
environmental_context: Primarily found on rocky outcrops and ridge formations
Often blends visually with terrain due to stone-like morphology
Best detected on exposed geological structures rather than flat plains

color_variants.rule: Color depends on parent star type (genus-wide deterministic rule)

Osseus cornibus.description: Horn-like branching structures adapted to CO2-rich cold environments.

Osseus discus.description: Wide disk-shaped mineral organism forming layered bio-rock plates.

Osseus fractus.description: Fragmented, broken crystalline formations resembling shattered rock spines.

Osseus pellebantus.description: Smooth, rounded mineral growths with dense external layering.

Osseus pumice.description: Lightweight porous structures resembling volcanic pumice stone formations.

Osseus spiralis.description: Coiled spiral-shaped mineral organism adapted to ammonia-rich environments.

special_rules: Extremely high minimum sample distance (800m) due to sparse clustering
Osseus structures blend heavily with terrain and are visually deceptive
Primary habitat is rocky ridges, outcrops, and elevated stone formations
CO2-based species require strict cold temperature ranges
Some variants prefer high metal content worlds (Osseus pumice)
Atmosphere is secondary filter; terrain visibility is primary detection factor
Osseus behaves more like mineralized bio-architecture than organic flora
